analysis.investment_thesis: Avanti Feeds has a pristine balance sheet and decent returns, but at 31.7x P/E it is priced well above my comfort range, and the shrimp feed business has demonstrated earnings volatility I find uncomfortable. I would wait for a meaningful correction before considering entry.
key_strengths: Fortress balance sheet — effectively zero debt (INR 15 Cr borrowings vs INR 3,011 Cr equity), a non-negotiable green flag
Solid capital returns — ROE 19.5% and ROCE 24% comfortably above my 18% floor; reserves compounding at healthy pace
Steady long-term revenue CAGR of 12.6% over 9 years fits my 10–15% steady-compounder preference
key_risks: Earnings volatility is unacceptable — operating income swung from INR 684 Cr (2018) down to INR 314 Cr (2022), a 54% collapse, signalling commodity/disease cycle exposure
Promoter holding at 43.23% is well below my 55% floor, reducing my confidence in long-term alignment
Valuation at 31.7x P/E and 6.67x P/B is far above my 12–20x comfort zone — I am being asked to pay a growth premium for a commodity-adjacent business
red_flags: Revenue growth has near-stalled in recent years: INR 5,036 Cr (2022) → INR 5,612 Cr (2025), barely 3.6% CAGR — raises questions about addressable market saturation
Other income of INR 166 Cr is now ~30% of net profit (INR 557 Cr) — core operating earnings quality is lower than headline PAT suggests
Free cash flow was deeply negative in 2022 (−INR 267 Cr); OCF positive only 4/5 years — inconsistency that concerns me
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Avanti Feeds is a market leader in Indian shrimp feed, and its balance sheet is genuinely excellent — near-zero debt, growing reserves from INR 1,390 Cr to INR 2,997 Cr in five years, and a ROCE of 24%. The 9-year revenue CAGR of 12.6% and net profit CAGR of 15% fit my steady-compounder template on paper. However, the shrimp feed business is fundamentally exposed to raw material prices (soybean meal, fishmeal), shrimp disease cycles, and aquaculture farmer economics — none of which are within my circle of competence or control. The 2018–2022 earnings collapse (operating income nearly halved) is exactly the kind of volatility I avoid.

At 31.7x P/E and 6.67x P/B, the market is pricing this as a premium FMCG business. I do not agree. Top-line growth has slowed sharply to under 4% CAGR over the last three years, and a meaningful portion of profits are now coming from financial income rather than core operations. Promoter holding at 43.23% gives me pause — I need promoters who act like owners. The stock may be a decent business, but it is not cheap enough to compensate for the cyclicality, the sector risk outside my expertise, and the softening revenue trajectory.
